decks.title: Continuity and Differentiability — Part 1: Continuity, discontinuity and differentiability
goals: Test the continuity of a function at a point with one-sided limits
Find constants that make a piecewise function continuous
Classify a discontinuity as removable, jump or infinite, and remove it when possible
Test the differentiability of a function at a point, including mod x and the greatest integer function
Use the fact that differentiability implies continuity

slides.heading: Continuity and Differentiability, Part 1
slides.body_md: When can you draw a graph without lifting the pen, and when does it have a smooth slope?

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: continuity at a point, continuity on an interval, the three kinds of discontinuity, differentiability, and the special functions mod x and greatest integer of x.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on continuity and differentiability. Think of drawing a graph without lifting your pen: that is continuity. Now think of a graph with no sharp corners: that is differentiability. In this part you will test both properties at a point, classify the breaks you find, and repair the ones that can be repaired.

slides.heading: Continuity at a point
slides.body_md: $f$ is **continuous at** $a$ when $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$.

rows: exist and equal the left-hand limit
be defined and equal both limits

visual.alt: Table of the three numbers in the test for continuity at a point: the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value, which must all exist and be equal.
visual.caption: Continuity at $a$: three numbers, one value.

slides.narration: Continuity at a point compares three numbers: the limit from the left, the limit from the right and the value of the function at the point. All three must exist and all three must be equal. If any one of them is missing or different, the function is discontinuous there.

slides.heading: Joining two pieces without a break
slides.body_md: $f(x) = kx^2 + 1$ for $x \le 3$ and $4x - 2$ for $x > 3$ meet when $9k + 1 = 10$.

visual.alt: Graph of a function made of two pieces: the parabola y equals x squared plus 1 up to x equals 3, and the line y equals 4 x minus 2 after it. Both pieces reach the point (3, 10), so the graph has no break there.
visual.caption: With $k = 1$ both pieces meet at $(3, 10)$.

slides.narration: A piecewise function is continuous at its join only if both pieces reach the same height there. On the left the curve reaches nine k plus one, on the right the line reaches ten. Setting these equal gives k equal to one, and the graph then passes through the point three, ten without a break.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: find the constant
slides.body_md: $f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + k, & x \le 3 \\ x^2 - 2, & x > 3 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x = 3$. Find $k$.

visual.alt: Worked example 1 table: the left-hand limit and the value are 6 plus k, the right-hand limit is 7, so k equals 1 for continuity at 3.
visual.caption: Set the two one-sided limits equal and solve.

slides.narration: Write each one-sided limit on its own line. From the left, and at the point itself, the first piece gives six plus k. From the right, the second piece gives seven. Continuity demands that these agree, so k equals one.

slides.heading: Algebra of continuous functions
slides.body_md: Sums, differences, products and composites of continuous functions are continuous; quotients too, where the denominator is not zero.

visual.alt: Table of the algebra of continuous functions: sums, differences, products and constant multiples are continuous; a quotient is continuous where the denominator is not zero; a composite is continuous when the outer function is continuous at the inner value.
visual.caption: Build continuity from simple pieces.

slides.narration: You rarely need limits to prove continuity of a formula. If two functions are continuous at a point, so are their sum, difference and product. Their quotient is continuous wherever the denominator is not zero, and a composite is continuous when each layer is. This is how we know rational functions are continuous on their domains.

slides.heading: Continuity on an interval
slides.body_md: A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every point of it (one-sided at closed ends).

visual.alt: Table of where standard functions are continuous: polynomials, sine, cosine and exponential on all reals; tangent and secant except odd multiples of pi by 2; log x for positive x; mod x everywhere; the greatest integer function except at integers.
visual.caption: Each is continuous at every point of its domain except $[x]$ at the integers.

slides.narration: A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point inside, and from the appropriate side at any closed end. Polynomials, sine, cosine and the exponential are continuous everywhere. The logarithm is continuous for positive x. The greatest integer function is the exception: it breaks at every integer.

slides.heading: Three kinds of discontinuity
slides.body_md: **Removable:** limit exists, value missing or different. **Jump:** finite one-sided limits that differ. **Infinite:** values grow without bound.

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of discontinuity: removable when the limit exists but the value is missing or different; jump when the one-sided limits are finite but unequal; infinite when a one-sided limit is infinite. Only the first can be removed.
visual.caption: Look at the one-sided limits first.

slides.narration: When continuity fails, look at the one-sided limits. If they agree, the break is removable: only the value is wrong or missing, and redefining it fixes everything. If they are finite but different, the graph jumps. If at least one of them is infinite, the graph shoots off. Jumps and infinite breaks cannot be removed.

slides.heading: A removable gap
slides.body_md: $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 16}{x - 4}$ equals $x + 4$ for $x \ne 4$; the stored value $g(4) = 5$ is wrong.

visual.alt: Graph of g of x equal to x squared minus 16 over x minus 4, which is the line y equals x plus 4 with the point at x equals 4 missing from the line; the stored value g of 4 equals 5 sits below the line, away from the height 8 that the line approaches.
visual.caption: The line approaches $8$ at $x = 4$, but the stored value is $5$: a removable discontinuity.

slides.narration: Here the formula simplifies to x plus four everywhere except at four. The graph is a straight line that approaches the height eight, but the stored value at four is five. The limit exists, so this is a removable discontinuity. Changing a single value, to eight, repairs it.

slides.heading: Quick check: what does removable mean?
slides.body_md: Choose the correct description of a removable discontinuity.
slides.narration: Ask yourself: does the limit exist at the point? What is wrong if the function is still discontinuous?

slides.heading: A jump
slides.body_md: $h(x) = \dfrac{|x - 1|}{x - 1}$ is $-1$ on the left and $1$ on the right of $x = 1$.

visual.alt: Graph of h of x equal to mod of x minus 1 over x minus 1: a horizontal segment at height minus 1 to the left of x equals 1 and a horizontal segment at height 1 to the right, with the value h of 1 equal to 1 marked. The graph jumps by 2 at x equals 1.
visual.caption: Left-hand limit $-1$, right-hand limit $1$: a jump.

slides.narration: This function is minus one to the left of one and plus one to the right. The one-sided limits are both finite but they are different, so the graph jumps by two. Whatever value you give at the point itself, one side will disagree with it, so a jump can never be removed.

slides.heading: An infinite break
slides.body_md: $\dfrac{1}{(x + 2)^2}$ grows without bound as $x \to -2$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 1 over x plus 2 squared: two branches that rise steeply on both sides of the vertical line x equals minus 2, passing through (minus 3, 1) and (minus 1, 1). The values grow without bound near minus 2.
visual.caption: Near $x = -2$ the values grow without bound: an infinite discontinuity.

slides.narration: Near minus two the denominator becomes tiny and positive, so the values shoot up without bound on both sides. No finite limit exists, so there is no number you could assign at minus two to make the function continuous. This is an infinite discontinuity.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify and repair
slides.body_md: $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - x - 6}{x - 3}$ for $x \ne 3$, $f(3) = 2$. Classify the discontinuity at $3$ and repair it.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 table: factorise x squared minus x minus 6, cancel x minus 3, find the limit 5, compare with the stored value 2, classify the break as removable and repair it by setting f of 3 equal to 5.
visual.caption: Factorise, cancel, take the limit, compare.

slides.narration: Factorise the numerator and cancel the common factor. The function behaves like x plus two near three, so the limit is five from both sides. The stored value is two, which disagrees. Since the limit exists, the discontinuity is removable, and setting the value at three equal to five repairs it.

slides.heading: Quick check: a reciprocal break
slides.body_md: Decide whether this break can be removed.
slides.narration: What happens to the values as x gets close to three from each side?

slides.heading: Differentiability at a point
slides.body_md: $f$ is **differentiable** at $a$ when the left-hand and right-hand derivatives exist and are equal.

visual.alt: Flow for testing differentiability at a point: find the left-hand derivative and the right-hand derivative; if they are finite and equal, the function is differentiable and the derivative is the common value.
visual.caption: Differentiable means the two one-sided slopes agree.

slides.narration: Differentiability is about slopes. Take the difference quotient with a small step on the left and on the right. If both one-sided derivatives exist and agree, the function is differentiable and the common value is the derivative. If the function is differentiable at a point, it must also be continuous there.

slides.heading: A corner: mod x
slides.body_md: $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ but its one-sided derivatives are $-1$ and $1$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals mod x: a V shape with its tip at the origin, slope minus 1 on the left through (minus 1, 1) and slope 1 on the right through (1, 1).
visual.caption: Continuous at $0$, but the slopes $-1$ and $1$ differ: a corner, not differentiable.

slides.narration: The graph of mod x has a sharp tip at the origin. You can draw it without lifting the pen, so it is continuous there. But the slope is minus one on the left and plus one on the right. The one-sided derivatives disagree, so mod x is not differentiable at zero. Continuity does not guarantee smoothness.

slides.heading: Steps: the greatest integer function
slides.body_md: $[x]$ jumps by $1$ at every integer, so it is neither continuous nor differentiable there.

visual.alt: Graph of the greatest integer function y equals greatest integer of x from 0 to 3: three flat steps at heights 0, 1 and 2, each starting at an integer, with the points (1, 1) and (2, 2) marked at the left ends of the upper steps.
visual.caption: Each step starts at an integer, where $[x]$ jumps by $1$.

slides.narration: The greatest integer function is a staircase. Between integers it is flat, so it is continuous and its derivative is zero. At each integer it jumps up by one, so it is not continuous there, and therefore not differentiable either.

slides.heading: Quick check: counting the steps
slides.body_md: Count the points of discontinuity of a step function on an interval.
slides.narration: Find the values of x where the expression inside the greatest integer bracket becomes a whole number.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a smooth join
slides.body_md: Find $a$, $b$ so that $f(x) = \begin{cases} ax^2 + 1, & x \le 1 \\ 3x + b, & x > 1 \end{cases}$ is differentiable at $x = 1$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 table: for a smooth join at x equals 1, no break gives a plus 1 equals 3 plus b, no corner gives 2 a equals 3, so a is three halves and b is minus one half.
visual.caption: Two conditions, two unknowns.

slides.narration: A smooth join needs two conditions. First, no break: the values on both sides must agree, giving a plus one equals three plus b. Second, no corner: the slopes must agree, giving two a equals three. So a is three halves and b is minus one half.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is smooth?
slides.body_md: Only one of four functions has a derivative at the origin.
slides.narration: Compute the slope just to the left and just to the right of zero for each function.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Continuous: left limit $=$ right limit $= f(a)$

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: continuity needs both one-sided limits equal to the value; breaks are removable, jumps or infinite; differentiability needs equal one-sided slopes; and differentiability implies continuity.
visual.caption: Part 1 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Continuity at a point needs both one-sided limits to equal the value. A break is removable when the limit exists, otherwise it is a jump or an infinite break. Differentiability needs equal one-sided derivatives, and it implies continuity, but mod x shows the converse fails.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the left-hand and right-hand limits **separately**

headers: How ISC marks are usually given

visual.alt: Exam tips table: finding k earns marks for the limits and the equation; classifying a discontinuity needs the limits, the type with reason and the repair; a differentiability test needs continuity and both one-sided derivatives; a smooth join needs a value equation and a slope equation.
visual.caption: Write each one-sided limit or derivative separately: each carries a mark.

slides.narration: In the examination, show each one-sided limit or derivative on its own line, because each carries a mark. When you classify a discontinuity, give the reason. Before testing differentiability, check continuity, because a break settles the question at once.

decks.title: Continuity and Differentiability — Part 2: Derivatives and the chain rule
goals: Differentiate trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
Apply the chain rule to composites with two or three layers
Differentiate a to the power x and logarithms of functions
Simplify by trigonometric substitution before differentiating, checking the principal range

slides.heading: Continuity and Differentiability, Part 2
slides.body_md: A short table of standard derivatives and one rule for layers let you differentiate almost anything in this chapter.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: standard derivatives, the chain rule, exponentials with any base and logarithms, inverse trigonometric derivatives, and trigonometric substitution.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. You already know how to differentiate powers. Now you will add the trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, and learn the chain rule, which handles a function inside another function. Then you will meet the inverse trigonometric functions and a powerful trick: substitute an angle before you differentiate.

slides.heading: Standard derivatives
slides.body_md: Every chain-rule answer is built from this table.

visual.alt: Table of standard derivatives: sine to cosine, cosine to minus sine, tangent to secant squared, secant to secant tangent, e to the x to itself, a to the x to a to the x times log a, log x to 1 over x, cosec to minus cosec cot.
visual.caption: Learn these by heart; the chain rule does the rest.

slides.narration: Here is the table you must know by heart. Sine gives cosine, cosine gives minus sine, tangent gives secant squared, and secant gives secant times tangent. The exponential e to the x is its own derivative, a to the x gains a factor log a, and log x gives one over x.

slides.heading: The exponential and the logarithm
slides.body_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log x = \dfrac{1}{x}$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals e to the x through (0, 1) and y equals log x through (1, 0), mirror images in the line y equals x. Each graph has slope 1 at its marked point.
visual.caption: At $(0, 1)$ the slope of $e^x$ is $1$; at $(1, 0)$ the slope of $\log x$ is $1$.

slides.narration: The graphs of e to the x and log x are mirror images in the line y equals x. The exponential has slope one where it crosses the vertical axis, and the logarithm has slope one where it crosses the horizontal axis. Their derivatives are e to the x and one over x.

slides.heading: The chain rule
slides.body_md: If $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f'(u)\,g'(x)$.

visual.alt: Flow of the chain rule: x goes into the inner function u equals g of x, then into the outer function y equals f of u; the derivative is the outer derivative at u times the inner derivative.
visual.caption: Differentiate from the outside in, multiplying as you go.

slides.narration: When one function sits inside another, differentiate the outer function, keep the inside unchanged, and multiply by the derivative of the inside. With three layers, keep multiplying. A common mistake is to forget the derivative of the innermost layer.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: three layers
slides.body_md: Differentiate $e^{\cos^2 x}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 table: for e to the power cos squared x, the outer exponential stays, the square gives 2 cos x, the cosine gives minus sin x; the product is minus sin 2 x times e to the cos squared x.
visual.caption: Three layers, three factors.

slides.narration: Peel the layers one at a time. The exponential keeps its form. The square gives two cos x. The cosine gives minus sin x. Multiply the three factors and use the double angle identity: the derivative is minus sin two x times e to the power cos squared x.

slides.heading: Quick check: a slope at the origin
slides.body_md: Find the slope of an exponential of a sine at the origin.
slides.narration: Differentiate with the chain rule and then substitute zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a root of a sum
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\sqrt{1 + e^{2x}}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 table: the square root contributes 1 over 2 root of 1 plus e to the 2 x, the inside contributes 2 e to the 2 x, and the product simplifies to e to the 2 x over root of 1 plus e to the 2 x.
visual.caption: Simplify the constants at the end.

slides.narration: The square root is the outer layer. Its derivative is one over two times the root. The inside, one plus e to the two x, has derivative two e to the two x. The twos cancel, leaving e to the two x over the root of one plus e to the two x.

slides.heading: Any base, and logarithms of functions
slides.body_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\log a$; $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log g(x) = \dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$.

visual.alt: Table of derivatives of composites with exponentials and logarithms: a to the g of x gives itself times log a times g dash; log of g of x gives g dash over g; e to the g of x gives itself times g dash.
visual.caption: Never use the power rule when the variable is in the exponent.

slides.narration: Write a to the x as e to the power x log a, and the derivative a to the x times log a follows. For the logarithm of a function, the derivative is the derivative of the inside divided by the inside. Never use the power rule when the variable sits in the exponent.

slides.heading: Quick check: a fixed base
slides.body_md: Choose the derivative of an exponential with base five.
slides.narration: Remember the extra factor that comes with a base other than e.

slides.heading: Inverse trigonometric derivatives
slides.body_md: Six results; the co-functions carry a minus sign.

visual.alt: Table of derivatives of the six inverse trigonometric functions: inverse sine, plus or minus 1 over root 1 minus x squared for inverse sine and cosine; 1 over 1 plus x squared with signs for inverse tangent and cotangent; 1 over mod x root x squared minus 1 with signs for inverse secant and cosecant.
visual.caption: The co-functions carry a minus sign.

slides.narration: The inverse sine has derivative one over the root of one minus x squared, and the inverse cosine has the same with a minus sign. The inverse tangent gives one over one plus x squared, and the inverse cotangent its negative. The inverse secant and cosecant involve mod x times the root of x squared minus one.

slides.heading: Inverse sine and its slope
slides.body_md: At $0$ the slope of $\sin^{-1} x$ is $1$; near $\pm 1$ it grows without bound.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals inverse sine of x from minus 1 to 1, rising from minus pi by 2 to pi by 2, with its tangent line y equals x at the origin. The curve becomes vertical at the ends, where the derivative is undefined.
visual.caption: Slope $1$ at the origin; the slope grows without bound as $x \to \pm 1$.

slides.narration: The graph of the inverse sine rises from minus a half pi to a half pi. At the origin its tangent is the line y equals x, so the slope is one. Towards the ends the curve becomes vertical, which matches the derivative growing without bound as x approaches plus or minus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: a constant sum
slides.body_md: Decide whether this statement about an inverse sine plus an inverse cosine is true.
slides.narration: Add the two standard derivatives. What do you notice about the sum itself?

slides.heading: Trigonometric substitution
slides.body_md: Recognise a pattern, substitute an angle, simplify with an identity, then check the principal range.

visual.alt: Table of trigonometric substitutions: root of 1 minus x squared suggests x equals sin theta; 1 plus x squared suggests x equals tan theta; the double-angle fractions become tan, sin or cos of 2 theta with x equals tan theta; 3 x minus 4 x cubed becomes sin 3 theta.
visual.caption: Then check that the new angle lies in the principal range.

slides.narration: Some inverse trigonometric expressions simplify dramatically after a substitution. A root of one minus x squared suggests x equals sin theta. A one plus x squared suggests x equals tan theta. Double angle fractions turn into tan, sin or cos of two theta. Always check that the new angle stays in the principal range.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: substitute first
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{1 + x^2} - 1}{x}\right)$, $x \ne 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6 table: put x equals tan theta, simplify the fraction to tan of theta by 2, check that theta by 2 lies between minus pi by 4 and pi by 4, so the function is half of inverse tan x, with derivative 1 over 2 times 1 plus x squared.
visual.caption: Substitute, simplify, check the range, then differentiate.

slides.narration: Direct differentiation would be messy. Put x equals tan theta. The root becomes sec theta, and the fraction simplifies to tan of half theta. Half theta lies in the principal range of the inverse tangent, so the function is just half of inverse tan x, and its derivative is one over two times one plus x squared.

slides.heading: Two formulas, one function

visual.alt: Graph on the interval from minus 1 to 1 of inverse tan of 2 x over 1 minus x squared and of 2 times inverse tan x: the two curves coincide, passing through the origin.
visual.caption: On $-1 < x < 1$ the two functions are the same, so they have the same derivative $\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$.

slides.narration: The graph shows that on the interval from minus one to one, the complicated expression and two times inverse tan x draw exactly the same curve. Equal functions on an interval have equal derivatives there, so the derivative is two over one plus x squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: the range matters
slides.body_md: Differentiate $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\right)$ for $|x| < 1$ and for $x > 1$.
bullets: $|x| < 1$: $2\theta$ in the principal range; derivative $\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$

visual.alt: Worked example 7 table: for inverse sine of 2 x over 1 plus x squared, when x is between minus 1 and 1 the function is 2 inverse tan x with derivative 2 over 1 plus x squared; when x is greater than 1 it is pi minus 2 inverse tan x with derivative minus 2 over 1 plus x squared.
visual.caption: The same formula has different derivatives on different intervals.

slides.narration: The same expression can simplify differently on different intervals. With x equals tan theta, the inside is sin two theta. When x lies between minus one and one, two theta is in the principal range and the function is two inverse tan x. When x is greater than one, it is pi minus two inverse tan x, and the sign of the derivative flips.

slides.heading: Quick check: a double-angle fraction
slides.body_md: Choose the derivative after the tangent substitution.
slides.narration: Simplify the fraction into a tangent of a double angle, check the range, then differentiate.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Learn the standard and inverse trigonometric tables
Chain rule: outer derivative times inner derivative

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 2: the standard table, the chain rule as outer derivative times inner derivative, a to the x giving a to the x log a, the inverse trigonometric table, and substitution followed by a range check.
visual.caption: Part 2 in one line.

slides.narration: To sum up. Two tables, the standard derivatives and the inverse trigonometric derivatives, combined with the chain rule, cover this part. A to the x brings a log a factor. For inverse trigonometric expressions, substitute an angle, simplify, check the principal range and only then differentiate.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Show each chain-rule factor before simplifying
Write the range check as a separate line
Do not apply the power rule to $a^x$ or $e^x$

headers: How ISC marks are usually given
rows: substitution and identity 1, range check 1, derivative 1
identity used, then derivative, for each part

visual.alt: Exam tips table for Part 2: chain-rule questions reward each layer and the simplified answer; substitution questions reward the identity, the range check and the derivative; simplify-first questions reward the identity and the derivative in each part; a to the x answers must show the log a factor.
visual.caption: The range check is a step of its own: write it.

slides.narration: In the examination, write each chain-rule factor before you simplify, because method marks follow the steps. In substitution questions, the range check is a step of its own, so write it. Do not use the power rule for exponentials, and keep the minus signs of the co-functions.

notes.title: Continuity and Differentiability — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Continuity at a point and on an interval
sections.body_md:
$f$ is **continuous at** $a$ if $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$. It is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of it (one-sided at closed ends).

For a piecewise function, only the joins need checking: set the one-sided limits equal to the value and solve for any constants. Standard limits help: $\dfrac{\sin u}{u} \to 1$, $\dfrac{e^u - 1}{u} \to 1$, $\dfrac{1 - \cos u}{u^2} \to \dfrac12$ as $u \to 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: Both one-sided limits exist and equal the value.
Continuous at every point of the interval.

rows: exist and equal the left-hand limit
be defined and equal both limits

visual.alt: Table of the three numbers in the test for continuity at a point: the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value, which must all exist and be equal.
visual.caption: Continuity at $a$: three numbers, one value.

visuals.alt: Graph of a function made of two pieces: the parabola y equals x squared plus 1 up to x equals 3, and the line y equals 4 x minus 2 after it. Both pieces reach the point (3, 10), so the graph has no break there.
visuals.caption: With $k = 1$ both pieces meet at $(3, 10)$.

sections.heading: 2. Algebra of continuous functions
sections.body_md:
If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $a$, then $f \pm g$, $fg$ and $cf$ are continuous at $a$; $\dfrac{f}{g}$ is continuous at $a$ if $g(a) \ne 0$; and $f \circ g$ is continuous at $a$ if $f$ is continuous at $g(a)$.

So polynomials, $\sin x$, $\cos x$ and $e^x$ are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$; rational functions, $\tan x$, $\sec x$ and $\log x$ are continuous on their domains. If $f$ is continuous at $a$ and $g$ is not, then $f + g$ is not continuous at $a$.

key_terms.definition_md: Sums, differences, products, quotients (non-zero denominator) and composites of continuous functions are continuous.

visual.alt: Table of the algebra of continuous functions: sums, differences, products and constant multiples are continuous; a quotient is continuous where the denominator is not zero; a composite is continuous when the outer function is continuous at the inner value.
visual.caption: Build continuity from simple pieces.

visuals.alt: Table of where standard functions are continuous: polynomials, sine, cosine and exponential on all reals; tangent and secant except odd multiples of pi by 2; log x for positive x; mod x everywhere; the greatest integer function except at integers.
visuals.caption: Each is continuous at every point of its domain except $[x]$ at the integers.

sections.heading: 3. Discontinuity and its types
sections.body_md:
- **Removable:** $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists but $f(a)$ is undefined (first type) or $f(a) \ne$ the limit (second type). Remove it by defining $f(a)$ = the limit.
- **Jump (non-removable):** the one-sided limits are finite but unequal.
- **Infinite (non-removable):** a one-sided limit is infinite, as for $\dfrac{1}{x - 3}$ at $3$.

Method: factorise and cancel, or use a standard limit, then compare the limits with the value.

key_terms.definition_md: The limit exists, but the value is missing or different from it.
Finite one-sided limits that are unequal.

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of discontinuity: removable when the limit exists but the value is missing or different; jump when the one-sided limits are finite but unequal; infinite when a one-sided limit is infinite. Only the first can be removed.
visual.caption: Look at the one-sided limits first.

visuals.alt: Graph of g of x equal to x squared minus 16 over x minus 4, which is the line y equals x plus 4 with the point at x equals 4 missing from the line; the stored value g of 4 equals 5 sits below the line, away from the height 8 that the line approaches.
visuals.caption: The line approaches $8$ at $x = 4$, but the stored value is $5$: a removable discontinuity.

visuals.alt: Graph of h of x equal to mod of x minus 1 over x minus 1: a horizontal segment at height minus 1 to the left of x equals 1 and a horizontal segment at height 1 to the right, with the value h of 1 equal to 1 marked. The graph jumps by 2 at x equals 1.
visuals.caption: Left-hand limit $-1$, right-hand limit $1$: a jump.

sections.heading: 4. Differentiability
sections.body_md:
Left-hand derivative $Lf'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0^-}\dfrac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$; right-hand derivative $Rf'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0^+}\dfrac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$. $f$ is **differentiable** at $a$ when both exist and are equal.

**Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous**, since $f(a + h) - f(a) = \dfrac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h} \cdot h \to 0$. The converse fails: $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ with one-sided derivatives $-1$ and $1$. $[x]$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at any integer. For a smooth join of two pieces, match both the values and the slopes.

key_terms.definition_md: Both one-sided derivatives exist and are equal.
A point of continuity where the one-sided derivatives differ.

visual.alt: Flow for testing differentiability at a point: find the left-hand derivative and the right-hand derivative; if they are finite and equal, the function is differentiable and the derivative is the common value.
visual.caption: Differentiable means the two one-sided slopes agree.

visuals.caption: Continuous at $0$, but the slopes $-1$ and $1$ differ: a corner, not differentiable.

visuals.caption: Each step starts at an integer, where $[x]$ jumps by $1$.

sections.heading: 5. Standard derivatives and the chain rule
sections.body_md:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec x = \sec x\tan x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\log a$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log x = \dfrac{1}{x}$.

**Chain rule:** if $y = f(u)$ and $u = g(x)$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f'(u)\,g'(x)$; for three layers multiply three factors. In particular $\dfrac{d}{dx}\log g(x) = \dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)}$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{g(x)} = e^{g(x)}g'(x)$.

key_terms.definition_md: Derivative of a composite = outer derivative (at the inner value) times inner derivative.

visual.alt: Table of standard derivatives: sine to cosine, cosine to minus sine, tangent to secant squared, secant to secant tangent, e to the x to itself, a to the x to a to the x times log a, log x to 1 over x, cosec to minus cosec cot.
visual.caption: Learn these by heart; the chain rule does the rest.

visuals.alt: Flow of the chain rule: x goes into the inner function u equals g of x, then into the outer function y equals f of u; the derivative is the outer derivative at u times the inner derivative.
visuals.caption: Differentiate from the outside in, multiplying as you go.

visuals.alt: Table of derivatives of composites with exponentials and logarithms: a to the g of x gives itself times log a times g dash; log of g of x gives g dash over g; e to the g of x gives itself times g dash.
visuals.caption: Never use the power rule when the variable is in the exponent.

sections.heading: 6. Inverse trigonometric derivatives and substitution
sections.body_md:
$\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1} x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1} x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$ ($|x| < 1$); $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1} x = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cot^{-1} x = -\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$; $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sec^{-1} x = \dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\operatorname{cosec}^{-1} x = -\dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}$ ($|x| > 1$).

**Substitution:** put $x = \sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ or $\tan\theta$ to turn the expression into a multiple angle, then use $\sin^{-1}(\sin\phi) = \phi$ only when $\phi$ is in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ (and similarly for the others). The interval decides the formula: $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2} = 2\tan^{-1} x$ for $|x| \le 1$ but $\pi - 2\tan^{-1} x$ for $x > 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: The range of values of an inverse trigonometric function, e.g. $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ for $\sin^{-1}$.

visual.alt: Table of derivatives of the six inverse trigonometric functions: inverse sine, plus or minus 1 over root 1 minus x squared for inverse sine and cosine; 1 over 1 plus x squared with signs for inverse tangent and cotangent; 1 over mod x root x squared minus 1 with signs for inverse secant and cosecant.
visual.caption: The co-functions carry a minus sign.

visuals.alt: Table of trigonometric substitutions: root of 1 minus x squared suggests x equals sin theta; 1 plus x squared suggests x equals tan theta; the double-angle fractions become tan, sin or cos of 2 theta with x equals tan theta; 3 x minus 4 x cubed becomes sin 3 theta.
visuals.caption: Then check that the new angle lies in the principal range.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How ISC marks are usually awarded**
- *Continuity with a constant (2 marks):* the two one-sided limits, then the equation and its solution.
- *Classifying a discontinuity (2–3 marks):* the limits, the type with its reason, and the repair if removable.
- *Differentiability (3–5 marks):* continuity first, then each one-sided derivative, then the conclusion.
- *Chain rule and substitution (2–3 marks):* each factor, or the substitution, the range check and the derivative.
- *Section D (5 marks):* questions come in parts such as 2 + 3; label each part.

**Common mistakes**
- Calling a corner a discontinuity: $|x|$ is continuous at $0$.
- Trying to remove a jump by redefining one value.
- Dropping the derivative of the innermost layer.
- Using the power rule on $5^x$ or $e^{x^2}$.
- Skipping the principal-range check after a substitution.

questions.stem_md: Using one-sided limits, a function $f$ defined on an open interval around $a$ is continuous at $x = a$ exactly when

options.text_md: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$, whatever the value $f(a)$

questions.solution_md: All three numbers must exist and agree. Equal one-sided limits alone allow a hole or a misplaced point; a defined value alone allows a jump; the left-hand limit alone ignores the right side.

questions.stem_md: A rule is pieced together as $f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^2 + 1, & x \le 3 \\ 4x - 2, & x > 3 \end{cases}$. For the two pieces to meet without a break at $x = 3$, the constant $k$ must be
questions.solution_md: Left-hand limit and value: $9k + 1$. Right-hand limit: $12 - 2 = 10$. So $9k + 1 = 10$ and $k = 1$.

questions.stem_md: Two functions $f$ and $g$ are both continuous at $x = a$. Which conclusion about combining them is always valid?

options.text_md: $f + g$ may fail to be continuous at $a$
$fg$ is continuous at $a$ only when $f(a) = g(a)$

questions.solution_md: Sums, differences, products and constant multiples of continuous functions are continuous; a quotient is continuous wherever the denominator is not zero. At a zero of $g$ the quotient is not even defined.

questions.stem_md: Counting carefully, at how many points of the open interval $(-2, 2)$ is the sum $h(x) = [x] + |x|$ discontinuous? Here $[x]$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$.
questions.solution_md: $|x|$ is continuous everywhere, so $h$ is discontinuous exactly where $[x]$ jumps: at the integers $-1$, $0$ and $1$ inside the interval. That is $3$ points.

questions.stem_md: The quotient $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 7x + 10}{x - 5}$ is undefined at $x = 5$. Which value assigned to $f(5)$ makes $f$ continuous there?
questions.solution_md: For $x \ne 5$, $\dfrac{(x - 2)(x - 5)}{x - 5} = x - 2 \to 3$. Assigning $f(5) = 3$ fills the gap.

questions.stem_md: Near the origin a function is given by $g(x) = \dfrac{\sin 3x}{\tan 2x}$ for $x \ne 0$. What must $g(0)$ be for $g$ to be continuous at $0$?
questions.solution_md: Write $\dfrac{\sin 3x}{\tan 2x} = \dfrac{\sin 3x}{3x} \cdot \dfrac{2x}{\tan 2x} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} \to 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{3}{2}$. So $g(0) = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: A function has a **removable** discontinuity at $x = a$ when

options.text_md: $f$ is continuous at $a$ but not differentiable there
$\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, but $f(a)$ is undefined or differs from the limit
the left-hand and right-hand limits at $a$ are finite but unequal

questions.solution_md: "Removable" means the limit exists, so redefining one value fixes the break. Unequal finite one-sided limits give a jump; unbounded values give an infinite discontinuity; a corner is not a discontinuity at all.

questions.stem_md: An imagined data logger records $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 16}{x - 4}$ for $x \ne 4$ but stores $g(4) = 5$ by mistake. At $x = 4$ the function $g$ has
questions.solution_md: For $x \ne 4$, $g(x) = x + 4 \to 8$ from both sides, but $g(4) = 5 \ne 8$. The limit exists, so the discontinuity is removable: set $g(4) = 8$.

questions.stem_md: Describe the behaviour at $x = 1$ of the sign-type function $h(x) = \dfrac{|x - 1|}{x - 1}$ ($x \ne 1$), $h(1) = 1$.

options.text_md: a jump: left-hand limit $-1$, right-hand limit $1$

questions.solution_md: For $x < 1$ the quotient is $-1$; for $x > 1$ it is $1$. Finite but unequal one-sided limits mean a jump, which no choice of $h(1)$ can remove.

questions.stem_md: On a graph of $p(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x + 2)^2}$, what kind of break appears at $x = -2$?
questions.solution_md: As $x \to -2$ from either side, $(x + 2)^2 \to 0^+$, so $p(x) \to +\infty$. No finite limit exists: an infinite discontinuity, which cannot be removed.

questions.stem_md: The cubic quotient $q(x) = \dfrac{x^3 - 27}{x - 3}$ is not defined at $3$. To remove this discontinuity, $q(3)$ should be defined as
Which implication between differentiability and continuity at a point $c$ holds for every real function?

options.text_md: Not differentiable at $c$ implies not continuous at $c$.
Continuous at $c$ implies the graph is smooth at $c$.

questions.solution_md: $f(c + h) - f(c) = \dfrac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h} \cdot h \to f'(b) \cdot 0 = 0$, so differentiability forces continuity. $|x|$ at $0$ shows the converse is false.

questions.stem_md: A V-shaped graph is given by $g(x) = |2x + 5|$. At its tip $x = -\dfrac{5}{2}$, the function is
questions.solution_md: Both one-sided limits are $0 = g\left(-\dfrac52\right)$. The slope is $-2$ on the left and $2$ on the right, so there is a corner and no derivative.

questions.stem_md: Only one of these functions has a derivative at $x = 0$. Which one?
questions.solution_md: For $x^2|x|$ both one-sided derivatives are $\lim \dfrac{h^2|h|}{h} = \lim h|h| = 0$. The other three have one-sided slopes $\mp 1$, $\mp 1$ and $0$, $2$ at the origin: corners.

questions.stem_md: For the greatest integer function $f(x) = [x]$, what can be said at $x = 2$?
questions.solution_md: Left-hand limit $1$, right-hand limit $2$: a jump, so $f$ is not continuous at $2$; a function that is not continuous cannot be differentiable.

questions.stem_md: The pieces $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + a, & x \le 1 \\ bx, & x > 1 \end{cases}$ are to join smoothly, with no break and no corner, at $x = 1$. The pair $(a, b)$ is
questions.solution_md: No break: $1 + a = b$. No corner: left slope $2x = 2$ equals right slope $b$, so $b = 2$ and $a = 1$.

questions.stem_md: An exponential growth factor is $e^{x^2 + 3x}$. Its derivative with respect to $x$ is
questions.solution_md: The exponential keeps its form and is multiplied by the derivative of the exponent, $2x + 3$. The power rule never applies to $e^{u}$.

questions.stem_md: For $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the logarithm of the cosine, $\log(\cos x)$, has derivative
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{\cos x} \cdot (-\sin x) = -\tan x$: derivative of the inside over the inside.

questions.stem_md: A quantity grows as $5^x$ with a fixed base. Its rate of change with respect to $x$ is
questions.solution_md: $5^x = e^{x\log 5}$, so its derivative is $e^{x\log 5} \cdot \log 5 = 5^x\log 5$. The power-rule answer treats the exponent as a constant.

questions.stem_md: Three layers sit inside $\sec^2 3x$: a square, a secant and $3x$. Its derivative is
questions.solution_md: $2\sec 3x \cdot (\sec 3x\tan 3x) \cdot 3 = 6\sec^2 3x\tan 3x$. Dropping the inner factor $3$ gives the second option.

questions.stem_md: The composite $\sin(\log x)$, $x > 0$, is differentiated and the result is evaluated at $x = 1$. The value is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(\log x) = \cos(\log x) \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}$. At $x = 1$: $\cos 0 \cdot 1 = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The inverse cotangent, $\cot^{-1} x$, is a decreasing function on $\mathbb{R}$. Its derivative is
questions.solution_md: $\cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} x$, so its derivative is $-\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$, negative as a decreasing function requires.

questions.stem_md: On the interval $x > 1$, which expression is the derivative of the inverse secant $\sec^{-1} x$?
questions.solution_md: $\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x}$, whose derivative is $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{x^2}}} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}$ for $x > 1$.

questions.stem_md: Using the substitution $x = \tan\theta$, the derivative of $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}\right)$ on $-1 < x < 1$ simplifies to
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} = \tan 2\theta$ with $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < 2\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so the function is $2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x$, with derivative $\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$.

questions.stem_md: With $x = \sin\theta$ and $-\dfrac12 < x < \dfrac12$, the function $\sin^{-1}(3x - 4x^3)$ reduces to a multiple of $\sin^{-1} x$. Its derivative is
questions.solution_md: $3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta = \sin 3\theta$, and $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < 3\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ here, so the function is $3\sin^{-1} x$ with derivative $\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$.

questions.stem_md: For negative $x$, the angle $\cos^{-1}(e^x)$ is differentiated with the chain rule. The result is
questions.solution_md: $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (e^x)^2}} \cdot e^x$. For $x < 0$, $0 < e^x < 1$, so the root is real.

**Reason (R):** Just to the left of $x = 1$ the function $[x]$ equals $0$, and at and just to the right of $x = 1$ it equals $1$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 1$.

**Reason (R):** $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x)$ exists, but $g(1)$ is not defined.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: For $x \ne 1$, $g(x) = x + 1 \to 2$, while $g(1)$ is undefined. That is exactly what "removable" means (define $g(1) = 2$), so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The function $f(x) = |x - 4|$ is continuous at $x = 4$.

**Reason (R):** Every function that is continuous at a point is differentiable at that point.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: both one-sided limits are $0 = f(4)$. R is false: $|x - 4|$ itself is continuous at $4$ but has slopes $-1$ and $1$ there.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For $-1 < x < 1$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2}\right) = \dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$.

**Reason (R):** With $x = \tan\theta$, $\dfrac{2x}{1 - x^2} = \tan 2\theta$, and $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < 2\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ when $-1 < x < 1$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: By R the function equals $2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x$ on this interval, whose derivative is $\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$. Both true; R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The function $e^x + \sin x$ is continuous at every real number.

**Reason (R):** The sum of two functions that are continuous on $\mathbb{R}$ is continuous on $\mathbb{R}$.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $e^x$ and $\sin x$ are continuous everywhere, and R (the algebra of continuous functions) gives A directly.

questions.stem_md: If $f$ is continuous at $a$ and $g$ is **not** continuous at $a$, then $f + g$ is not continuous at $a$.
questions.solution_md: True. If $f + g$ were continuous at $a$, then $g = (f + g) - f$ would be a difference of continuous functions and hence continuous, a contradiction.

questions.stem_md: A function that fails to be differentiable at a point cannot be continuous at that point.
questions.solution_md: False. $|x|$ is continuous at $0$ but has a corner there, so it is not differentiable. Only the reverse implication holds.

questions.stem_md: On $-1 < x < 1$, the sum $\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x$ has derivative $0$.
questions.solution_md: True. $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = 0$; indeed the sum is the constant $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: The reciprocal function $\dfrac{1}{x - 3}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x = 3$.
questions.solution_md: False. As $x \to 3$ the values grow without bound ($-\infty$ on the left, $+\infty$ on the right): an infinite discontinuity, which no single value can repair.

questions.stem_md: The quotient $\dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{x}$ is undefined at $0$. To remove this discontinuity, its value at $0$ should be defined as ___.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{x} = 2 \cdot \dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{2x} \to 2 \cdot 1 = 2$.

questions.stem_md: If $y = e^{\sin 2x}$, the slope $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ at $x = 0$ equals ___.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{\sin 2x} \cdot 2\cos 2x$, which is $1 \cdot 2 = 2$ at $x = 0$.

questions.stem_md: For $y = \log(x^2 + 1)$, the derivative at $x = 1$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$, which is $\dfrac{2}{2} = 1$ at $x = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The step function $f(x) = [2x]$ is discontinuous at exactly ___ points of the open interval $(0, 2)$.
questions.solution_md: $[2x]$ jumps whenever $2x$ is an integer, that is at $x = \dfrac12, 1, \dfrac32$ inside the interval: $3$ points.

questions.stem_md: A cosine quotient is completed at the origin: $f(x) = \dfrac{1 - \cos 6x}{x^2}$ for $x \ne 0$ and $f(0) = k$. Find $k$ for continuity at $0$.
questions.solution_md: $1 - \cos 6x = 2\sin^2 3x$, so $f(x) = 18\left(\dfrac{\sin 3x}{3x}\right)^2 \to 18$. Hence $k = 18$.

questions.stem_md: Rationalise to find the value $a$ that makes $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x + 4} - 2}{x}$ ($x \ne 0$), $f(0) = a$, continuous at the origin.
questions.solution_md: Multiply by $\sqrt{x + 4} + 2$: $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x + 4} + 2} \to \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$. So $a = 0.25$.

questions.stem_md: A fifth power of a quadratic, $f(x) = (2x^2 - 3)^5$, is differentiated. Find $f'(1)$.
Find the slope of $y = \tan^{-1}(3x)$ where it crosses the origin.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3}{1 + 9x^2}$, which equals $3$ at $x = 0$.

questions.stem_md: The function $2^x$ is differentiated at $x = 0$. Give the value correct to three decimal places.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}2^x = 2^x\log 2$, so at $x = 0$ the value is $\log 2 \approx 0.693$.

questions.stem_md: A "distance to two posts" function is $f(x) = |x - 1| + |x - 3|$. At how many real points is it **not** differentiable?
questions.solution_md: Corners can occur only where an absolute value changes sign: $x = 1$ (slopes $-2$ and $0$) and $x = 3$ (slopes $0$ and $2$). Elsewhere $f$ is linear. So $2$ points.

questions.stem_md: A three-part rule is $f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x - 2, & x < 2 \\ 4, & x = 2 \\ x^2, & x > 2 \end{cases}$. Test whether it is continuous at $x = 2$.

answer.model_answer_md: Left-hand limit: $3(2) - 2 = 4$. Right-hand limit: $2^2 = 4$. Value: $f(2) = 4$. All three agree, so $f$ is **continuous** at $x = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Compare both one-sided limits with the value.

questions.stem_md: A rule is recorded as $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2, & x < 1 \\ 2, & x = 1 \\ 2x - 1, & x > 1 \end{cases}$. Classify the discontinuity at $x = 1$ and say how to remove it if possible.

answer.model_answer_md: Left-hand limit $1^2 = 1$; right-hand limit $2(1) - 1 = 1$. The limit exists and equals $1$, but $f(1) = 2$. So the discontinuity is **removable**: redefine $f(1) = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Equal one-sided limits with a different value means removable.

questions.stem_md: Find $k$ if the sine quotient $f(x) = \dfrac{\sin kx}{3x}$ for $x \ne 0$, with $f(0) = 2$, is continuous at the origin.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{\sin kx}{3x} = \dfrac{k}{3} \cdot \dfrac{\sin kx}{kx} \to \dfrac{k}{3}$. Continuity needs $\dfrac{k}{3} = 2$, so $k = 6$.

questions.solution_md: Use $\dfrac{\sin u}{u} \to 1$.

questions.stem_md: Show that the V-shaped function $g(x) = |2x - 3|$ is not differentiable at $x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $g\left(\dfrac32\right) = 0$. For $h > 0$: $\dfrac{|2h| - 0}{h} = 2$, so the right-hand derivative is $2$. For $h < 0$: $\dfrac{|2h|}{h} = -2$, so the left-hand derivative is $-2$. Since $-2 \ne 2$, $g$ is **not differentiable** at $\dfrac32$.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate $\log\left(\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$ with respect to $x$ for $0 < x < \pi$, and simplify.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{1}{\tan\frac{x}{2}} \cdot \sec^2\dfrac{x}{2} \cdot \dfrac12 = \dfrac{\cos\frac{x}{2}}{\sin\frac{x}{2}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\cos^2\frac{x}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sin x} = \operatorname{cosec} x$.

questions.solution_md: Chain rule through log, tan and x/2, then the double-angle identity.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate the cube $\cos^3 4x$ with respect to $x$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^3 4x = 3\cos^2 4x \cdot (-\sin 4x) \cdot 4 = -12\cos^2 4x\sin 4x$.

questions.solution_md: Power, then cosine, then 4x.

questions.stem_md: For $x < 0$, find the derivative of the composite angle $\sin^{-1}(e^x)$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}(e^x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (e^x)^2}} \cdot e^x = \dfrac{e^x}{\sqrt{1 - e^{2x}}}$, valid since $0 < e^x < 1$ for $x < 0$.

questions.solution_md: Inverse sine derivative with the chain rule.

questions.stem_md: Use $x = \tan\theta$ to simplify $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}\right)$ for $x < 1$, and hence differentiate it.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{1 + \tan\theta}{1 - \tan\theta} = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \theta\right)$, and for $x < 1$, $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} < \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So the function is $\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \tan^{-1} x$, with derivative $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$.

questions.stem_md: A damped signal is $s(x) = e^{-x}\cos x$. Find $\dfrac{ds}{dx}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Product rule: $\dfrac{ds}{dx} = -e^{-x}\cos x + e^{-x}(-\sin x) = -e^{-x}(\cos x + \sin x)$.

questions.solution_md: Product rule with the chain rule on the exponential.

questions.stem_md: Explain, using the algebra of continuous functions, why $r(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x^2 - 9}$ is continuous at every real number except $\pm 3$.

answer.model_answer_md: The numerator and denominator are polynomials, which are continuous everywhere. A quotient of continuous functions is continuous wherever the denominator is non-zero. Here $x^2 - 9 = 0$ only at $x = 3$ and $x = -3$, where $r$ is not defined. So $r$ is continuous at every other real number.

questions.solution_md: Polynomials are continuous; quotients fail only at zeros of the denominator.

marking_scheme.step: Polynomials continuous; quotient rule for continuity

questions.stem_md: Determine the constants $a$ and $b$ for which the three-piece function $f(x) = \begin{cases} 3, & x \le -1 \\ ax + b, & -1 < x < 3 \\ 11, & x \ge 3 \end{cases}$ has no break anywhere on the real line.

answer.model_answer_md: Each piece is continuous, so only the joins $x = -1$ and $x = 3$ matter. At $x = -1$: $-a + b = 3$. At $x = 3$: $3a + b = 11$. Subtracting, $4a = 8$, so $a = 2$ and $b = 5$.

questions.solution_md: Equate one-sided limits at both joins.

questions.stem_md: For $f(x) = |x| + |x - 2|$, show that $f$ is continuous at $x = 2$ but not differentiable there.

answer.model_answer_md: $f(2) = 2$. Near $x = 2$ with $x > 0$: for $0 < x < 2$, $f(x) = x + (2 - x) = 2$; for $x > 2$, $f(x) = 2x - 2$. Both one-sided limits are $2 = f(2)$, so $f$ is continuous at $2$. The left-hand derivative is $0$ (constant piece) and the right-hand derivative is $2$; they differ, so $f$ is **not differentiable** at $x = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Write f without absolute values on each side of 2.

questions.stem_md: On $[0, 2)$ consider $f(x) = x[x]$, where $[x]$ is the greatest integer function. Examine the continuity and differentiability of $f$ at $x = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md: For $0 \le x < 1$, $[x] = 0$, so $f(x) = 0$; for $1 \le x < 2$, $[x] = 1$, so $f(x) = x$. Left-hand limit at $1$: $0$. Right-hand limit and value: $f(1) = 1$. Since $0 \ne 1$, $f$ is **not continuous** at $1$ (a jump), and therefore **not differentiable** there.

questions.solution_md: Rewrite f piece by piece using the value of [x].

questions.stem_md: An imagined spreadsheet formula gives $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 3x - 10}{x + 2}$ for $x \ne -2$ and returns $f(-2) = 1$. Classify the discontinuity at $x = -2$ and redefine $f(-2)$ to make $f$ continuous.

answer.model_answer_md: $x^2 - 3x - 10 = (x - 5)(x + 2)$, so for $x \ne -2$, $f(x) = x - 5 \to -7$ from both sides. The limit exists but $f(-2) = 1 \ne -7$: a **removable** discontinuity. Redefining $f(-2) = -7$ makes $f$ continuous at $-2$.

questions.solution_md: Factorise, cancel, take the limit, compare with the stored value.

questions.stem_md: Find $a$ and $b$ so that $f(x) = \begin{cases} ax^2 + b, & x < 1 \\ 4x - 1, & x \ge 1 \end{cases}$ is differentiable at $x = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md: Differentiability needs continuity: $a + b = 4 - 1 = 3$. It also needs equal one-sided derivatives: $2a(1) = 4$, so $a = 2$. Then $b = 1$. With $a = 2$, $b = 1$ both pieces give value $3$ and slope $4$ at $x = 1$.

questions.solution_md: Two conditions: matching values and matching slopes.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate the root of a tangent, $\sqrt{\tan 3x}$, for $0 < x < \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{\tan 3x} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{\tan 3x}} \cdot \sec^2 3x \cdot 3 = \dfrac{3\sec^2 3x}{2\sqrt{\tan 3x}}$.

questions.solution_md: Root, then tangent, then 3x.

questions.stem_md: A product of an exponential and an inverse sine, $e^x\sin^{-1} x$, is differentiated on $-1 < x < 1$. Find the derivative.

answer.model_answer_md: Product rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^x\sin^{-1} x\right) = e^x\sin^{-1} x + e^x \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} = e^x\left(\sin^{-1} x + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}\right)$.

questions.solution_md: Product rule with the standard inverse-sine derivative.

questions.stem_md: With the substitution $x = \sin\theta$, differentiate $\sin^{-1}\left(2x\sqrt{1 - x^2}\right)$ on $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < x < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

answer.model_answer_md: Let $x = \sin\theta$ with $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Then $2x\sqrt{1 - x^2} = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin 2\theta$, and $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < 2\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So the function is $2\theta = 2\sin^{-1} x$, and its derivative is $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute, simplify with the double angle, check the principal range, differentiate.

questions.stem_md: For $0 < x < 1$, simplify $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1 - x^2}{1 + x^2}\right)$ by putting $x = \tan\theta$, and then find its derivative.

answer.model_answer_md: With $x = \tan\theta$, $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$: $\dfrac{1 - \tan^2\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \cos 2\theta$ and $0 < 2\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, inside $[0, \pi]$. So the function is $2\theta = 2\tan^{-1} x$, and its derivative is $\dfrac{2}{1 + x^2}$.

questions.solution_md: Substitute, use the cos 2θ identity, check the principal range.

questions.stem_md: Show that the derivative of $\log\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \sin x}{1 - \sin x}}$ on $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is $\sec x$.

answer.model_answer_md: The function is $\dfrac12\left[\log(1 + \sin x) - \log(1 - \sin x)\right]$. Differentiating: $\dfrac12\left[\dfrac{\cos x}{1 + \sin x} + \dfrac{\cos x}{1 - \sin x}\right] = \dfrac12 \cdot \dfrac{2\cos x}{1 - \sin^2 x} = \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos^2 x} = \sec x$.

questions.solution_md: Use log laws first, then differentiate each logarithm.

questions.stem_md:
A rule is defined by $f(x) = \begin{cases} kx^2, & x \le 2 \\ 3x + 4, & x > 2 \end{cases}$.

(a) Find $k$ so that $f$ is continuous at $x = 2$. [2]

(b) With this $k$, find both one-sided derivatives at $x = 2$ and decide whether $f$ is differentiable there. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Left-hand limit and value: $4k$. Right-hand limit: $3(2) + 4 = 10$. So $4k = 10$ and $k = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

(b) Left-hand derivative: $\lim_{h \to 0^-}\dfrac{\frac52(2 + h)^2 - 10}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-}\dfrac{10h + \frac52h^2}{h} = 10$. Right-hand derivative: $\lim_{h \to 0^+}\dfrac{3(2 + h) + 4 - 10}{h} = 3$. Since $10 \ne 3$, $f$ is continuous but **not differentiable** at $x = 2$.

questions.solution_md: Continuity fixes k; then compare the one-sided difference quotients.

questions.stem_md:
Consider $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x^2 - 3x + 2}$.

(a) Find the points where $f$ is discontinuous and classify each discontinuity. [3]

(b) Redefine $f$ at the removable point so that it becomes continuous there, and explain why the other discontinuity cannot be removed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2)$, so $f$ is undefined, hence discontinuous, at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. For $x \ne 1, 2$: $f(x) = \dfrac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{(x - 1)(x - 2)} = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 2}$.
At $x = 1$: the limit is $\dfrac{2}{-1} = -2$, which exists: a **removable** discontinuity.
At $x = 2$: the denominator tends to $0$ while the numerator tends to $3$, so $|f(x)| \to \infty$: an **infinite** discontinuity.

(b) Define $f(1) = -2$; then the limit and the value agree. At $x = 2$ no finite limit exists, so no choice of $f(2)$ can make $f$ continuous there.

questions.solution_md: Factorise both quadratics, cancel the common factor, and examine each zero of the denominator.

questions.stem_md:
Let $f(x) = |x - 1| + |x + 2|$.

(a) Write $f$ without absolute-value signs on the intervals $x < -2$, $-2 \le x \le 1$ and $x > 1$. [2]

(b) Show that $f$ is continuous at $x = 1$ and at $x = -2$, and find the one-sided derivatives at both points. State where $f$ is not differentiable. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) For $x < -2$: $f(x) = (1 - x) + (-x - 2) = -2x - 1$. For $-2 \le x \le 1$: $f(x) = (1 - x) + (x + 2) = 3$. For $x > 1$: $f(x) = (x - 1) + (x + 2) = 2x + 1$.

(b) At $x = -2$: $-2(-2) - 1 = 3 = f(-2)$, so continuous; slopes $-2$ (left) and $0$ (right). At $x = 1$: $2(1) + 1 = 3 = f(1)$, so continuous; slopes $0$ (left) and $2$ (right). The one-sided derivatives differ at both points, so $f$ is **not differentiable at $x = -2$ and $x = 1$**, and differentiable everywhere else.

questions.solution_md: Remove the absolute values interval by interval, then compare values and slopes at the joins.

questions.stem_md:
Inverse trigonometric derivatives by substitution.

(a) For $-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} < x < \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, differentiate $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3x - x^3}{1 - 3x^2}\right)$. [2]

(b) For $x < 0$, differentiate $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2^{x + 1}}{1 + 4^x}\right)$. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Put $x = \tan\theta$, $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{6}$: $\dfrac{3\tan\theta - \tan^3\theta}{1 - 3\tan^2\theta} = \tan 3\theta$ with $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < 3\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So the function is $3\theta = 3\tan^{-1} x$ and its derivative is $\dfrac{3}{1 + x^2}$.

(b) Put $2^x = \tan\theta$; for $x < 0$, $0 < \tan\theta < 1$, so $0 < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Then $\dfrac{2^{x + 1}}{1 + 4^x} = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \sin 2\theta$ with $0 < 2\theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So the function is $2\theta = 2\tan^{-1}(2^x)$, and its derivative is $\dfrac{2 \cdot 2^x\log 2}{1 + 4^x}$.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined auto-rickshaw tariff in Guwahati charges $F(d) = 40 + 12d$ rupees for a ride of $d$ km when $0 \le d \le 5$, and $F(d) = a + 15d$ rupees when $d > 5$.

(a) Find $a$ so that the fare has no sudden jump at $d = 5$. [2]

(b) With this $a$, is $F$ differentiable at $d = 5$? Find the one-sided rates and interpret your answer for a passenger. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Left-hand limit and value: $40 + 12(5) = 100$. Right-hand limit: $a + 75$. No jump needs $a + 75 = 100$, so $a = 25$.

(b) For $d < 5$ the fare rises at ₹$12$ per km; for $d > 5$ at ₹$15$ per km. The left-hand derivative at $5$ is $12$ and the right-hand derivative is $15$. They differ, so $F$ is continuous but **not differentiable** at $d = 5$: the fare has no jump there, but each extra kilometre beyond $5$ km costs ₹$3$ more than before.

questions.solution_md: Continuity fixes a; the two per-km rates are the one-sided derivatives.

questions.stem_md:
Simplify first, then differentiate.

(a) Differentiate $\dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$ for $-\pi < x < \pi$, giving the answer in terms of $\dfrac{x}{2}$. [2]

(b) Show that $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}\right) = \tan^{-1} x$ for all real $x$, and hence find its derivative. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x} = \dfrac{2\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2}}{2\cos^2\frac{x}{2}} = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}$, so its derivative is $\dfrac12\sec^2\dfrac{x}{2}$.

(b) Put $x = \tan\theta$ with $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Then $\sqrt{1 + x^2} = \sec\theta$ (positive in this range) and $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}} = \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sec\theta} = \sin\theta$. Since $\theta$ lies in the principal range of $\sin^{-1}$, the function equals $\theta = \tan^{-1} x$. Its derivative is $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$.

questions.solution_md: Half-angle identities in (a); a tangent substitution in (b).
